m7-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “AI ethics principles & real-world failures”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: FATE turns a principle into a review question
sections.explanation: Fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics need evidence in the actual use context. A policy slogan alone is not a safeguard.

items.label: Fairness
items.detail: Investigate unjustified differences and barriers for affected groups.

items.label: Accountability
items.detail: Assign an owner, correction process and human appeal route.

items.label: Transparency
items.detail: Explain the AI’s role, evidence and meaningful limitations.

items.label: Ethical purpose
items.detail: Ask whether the proposed use is appropriate at all.

sections.takeaway: Name the people affected and the remedy available when the system is wrong.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Harm can enter at data, design or use
sections.explanation: A technically accurate model can still be part of a harmful system if its objective or deployment is wrong.

items.label: Data
items.detail: Inspect coverage, labels and proxy variables.

items.label: Design
items.detail: Check the objective, interface, permissions and missing safeguards.

items.label: Use
items.detail: Look for overreliance, changed purpose and effects at scale.

items.label: Remedy
items.detail: Provide a way to question, correct or stop the harm.

sections.takeaway: Review organisational choices instead of blaming an abstract algorithm.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: The setting changes the consequences
sections.explanation: The lesson’s five settings illustrate why an error needs a contextual harm review, not only a performance score.

items.label: Hiring
items.detail: Unsupported screening can exclude people from opportunity.

items.label: Lending and insurance
items.detail: Proxy-driven decisions can affect access to resources.

items.label: Policing and surveillance
items.detail: Misidentification can affect liberty and lawful activity.

items.label: Exam proctoring
items.detail: A flag can become a false accusation without fair human review.

items.label: Moderation and recommendation
items.detail: Language gaps and ranking objectives can affect speech and wellbeing.

sections.takeaway: For a real case study, open primary evidence; these category labels do not establish a finding about a particular organisation.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: An ethics analysis ends with a decision
sections.explanation: Start from purpose and affected people, investigate harm and alternatives, then state an accountable recommendation.

items.label: Scope and stakeholders
items.detail: Name the system, use and everyone materially affected.

items.label: Harm and sources
items.detail: Identify potential consequences and their data, design or use causes.

items.label: Controls and alternatives
items.detail: Consider human review, appeal and a simpler or no-AI option.

items.label: Decision and ownership
items.detail: Proceed, redesign or stop with reasons and review conditions.

sections.takeaway: “Proceed with conditions” is meaningful only when the conditions, owners and review evidence are explicit.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Apply the same scrutiny to your own build
sections.explanation: A course project is not exempt from harm because it is small or well-intentioned.

items.label: Trace one user path
items.detail: Follow a real task from input to result.

items.label: Ask who could lose
items.detail: Consider a wrong answer, misclassification or exposed file.

items.label: Test the safeguard
items.detail: Check the approval, access and recovery behaviour.

items.label: Record and improve
items.detail: Fix the gap or narrow the permitted use.

sections.takeaway: An honest discovered weakness and correction is stronger evidence than an unsupported “all safe” claim.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Is a high technical accuracy score enough to approve an AI use case?
checkpoint.answer: No. Purpose, authority, affected people, fairness, privacy, error consequences, alternatives and remedies must also be reviewed.

m7-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “Detecting and reducing bias — hands-on”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Bias can enter before and after the model
sections.explanation: Representation, labelling, objectives, proxies and deployment context can each create unfair effects.

items.label: Representation
items.detail: Some contexts or languages may be poorly covered.

items.label: Labels
items.detail: Human judgements used as targets can embed bias.

items.label: Objectives
items.detail: A convenient measured goal may differ from the real need.

items.label: Proxies
items.detail: Other fields can carry correlated information.

items.label: Deployment
items.detail: A new population or use can change the consequences.

sections.takeaway: Removing a visible attribute does not prove that all proxies or historical disadvantages disappeared.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A paired test changes one deliberate signal
sections.explanation: Use controlled synthetic variants and a written coding scheme to investigate systematic differences.

items.label: Specify the test
items.detail: Define the use, synthetic variants and evaluation criteria.

items.label: Hold context fixed
items.detail: Change only the intended test signal between paired prompts.

items.label: Repeat and code
items.detail: Record all runs with consistent human review.

items.label: Compare and qualify
items.detail: Show differences, uncertainty and what the small test cannot establish.

sections.takeaway: Do not infer real people’s caste, religion or other sensitive traits from names or appearance. Synthetic test signals are not verified identities.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Fairness definitions answer different questions
sections.explanation: Equal rules, outcome rates and error rates focus on different aspects of treatment. Trade-offs depend on the population and decision.

items.label: Same rule
items.detail: Ask whether the process uses consistent relevant criteria.

items.label: Outcome comparison
items.detail: Inspect group access and selection patterns with context.

items.label: Error comparison
items.detail: Review the consequences of mistakes where valid outcomes exist.

items.label: Context and authority
items.detail: Choose and justify the evaluation with qualified reviewers.

sections.takeaway: Do not claim a universal fairness guarantee from one metric or one preferred target.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Mitigation needs more than a better prompt
sections.explanation: A prompt change can help one symptom but may leave the underlying data, objective or process harm unchanged.

items.label: Identify the mechanism
items.detail: Use evidence to understand where the problem enters.

items.label: Change the control
items.detail: Adjust data, process, interface or the permitted use.

items.label: Retest relevant cases
items.detail: Include languages and contexts that were missed.

items.label: Monitor and remediate
items.detail: Assign an owner, appeal path and review date.

sections.takeaway: Retest the actual workflow, keep a human remedy and refuse a use whose serious harms cannot be controlled.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A bias report links findings to action
sections.explanation: A reviewable report includes the method, examples, affected people and limitations as well as a recommendation.

items.label: Describe the method
items.detail: Record synthetic variants, runs and coding rules.

items.label: Show findings
items.detail: Keep examples and counts traceable to the test sheet.

items.label: Judge consequences
items.detail: Explain who may be harmed and under which use.

items.label: Recommend and retest
items.detail: Name a proportionate action, owner and remaining uncertainty.

sections.takeaway: The model under test should not be the sole judge of whether its own outputs are biased.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Does deleting names from input prove a screening process is fair?
checkpoint.answer: No. Other fields can act as proxies, historical patterns can remain, and the objective or process may still produce harm. Test the relevant use and provide human accountability.

m7-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “Explainability, model cards & transparency”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: An opaque result is hard to question or repair
sections.explanation: A result becomes operationally risky when nobody can inspect its basis, correct data or take responsibility.

items.label: Understand the basis
items.detail: Identify evidence, intended use and known limits.

items.label: Enable a challenge
items.detail: Give affected people a meaningful correction or review route.

items.label: Debug failures
items.detail: Keep appropriate logs and inspect changed behaviour.

items.label: Own the decision
items.detail: Name who may approve, override or withdraw the use.

sections.takeaway: A vendor’s model does not remove the deploying organisation’s duty to review its actual use.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Why black boxes are a business risk

sections.title: Explain for the stakeholder’s actual question
sections.explanation: Different audiences need different levels of detail, but every explanation must be accurate and appropriate for access.

items.label: Affected person
items.detail: Explain the relevant outcome and how to seek correction.

items.label: Operator
items.detail: Show supporting inputs, boundaries and override conditions.

items.label: Manager or auditor
items.detail: Provide aggregate behaviour, tests and remaining risks.

items.label: Qualified reviewer
items.detail: Keep appropriate documentation for the specific oversight process.

sections.takeaway: Do not expose someone else’s private data while trying to make a decision transparent.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. Who needs what kind of explanation

sections.title: Attribution is not a causal story
sections.explanation: Local surrogate methods and feature-contribution methods describe aspects of model behaviour under assumptions.

items.label: Local approximation
items.detail: A simple model can approximate behaviour near one case.

items.label: Feature contribution
items.detail: A method can allocate a prediction difference relative to a chosen baseline.

items.label: Method limitations
items.detail: Correlated inputs, background choices and local instability matter.

items.label: Human interpretation
items.detail: Check suitability and avoid overclaiming what the explanation proves.

sections.takeaway: An importance value does not establish causation, truth of an input or a lawful decision.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: An LLM’s self-explanation is another generated answer
sections.explanation: A chatbot does not provide a guaranteed faithful trace of its internal computation when asked why it answered.

items.label: Receive the explanation
items.detail: Treat it as a claim about the answer.

items.label: Inspect cited inputs
items.detail: Check that the supporting passage or field actually exists.

items.label: Test the claim
items.detail: Reproduce the relevant calculation or compare controlled cases.

items.label: Keep the uncertainty
items.detail: Do not claim access to a verified internal reasoning trace.

sections.takeaway: Use inspectable evidence and reproducible tests rather than treating a persuasive explanation as proof.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Read a card for relevance, not reassurance
sections.explanation: A model or system card is useful when its use scope and evaluations match your proposed workflow.

items.label: Check intended use
items.detail: Compare the documented and proposed tasks.

items.label: Inspect evaluations
items.detail: Look for languages, groups, sample conditions and limitations.

items.label: Review controls
items.detail: Identify known hazards and operational safeguards.

items.label: Record gaps
items.detail: Request evidence or decline a use when a material question is unanswered.

sections.takeaway: Published documentation is not independent certification of your deployment.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. Reading model cards and system cards

sections.title: Transparency includes a route to correction
sections.explanation: A disclosure label, source link, system description and human contact help different parts of accountability.

items.label: Disclose AI
items.detail: State what the automated feature does.

items.label: Show evidence
items.detail: Link relevant sources or input-tied reasons.

items.label: Document the system
items.detail: Record components, tests and limits.

items.label: Provide recourse
items.detail: Name an accessible human review and correction route.

sections.takeaway: Do not promise more explanation, recourse or reliability than the workflow actually provides.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can a feature-importance chart prove that a factor caused a real-world outcome?
checkpoint.answer: No. It describes model behaviour under assumptions, not necessarily causation. The data, method and actual decision context still need review.

m7-t4.introduction: A second way to understand “Security, privacy law & AI governance”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: A security boundary must exist outside the prompt
sections.explanation: Untrusted content, excessive tool permissions and exposed records can combine into a harmful workflow.

items.label: Minimise exposure
items.detail: Keep secrets and unnecessary personal data out of inputs and logs.

items.label: Enforce permission
items.detail: Limit data and tools to the authorised purpose.

items.label: Validate outputs
items.detail: Check structured results and source support independently.

items.label: Contain effects
items.detail: Use human gates, monitoring and a tested stop path.

sections.takeaway: Do not rely on model obedience to protect credentials, confidential documents or irreversible actions.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A privacy framework needs a current, contextual review
sections.explanation: Data handling depends on actual purpose, parties, retention, safeguards and applicable commencement provisions. This is a review map, not legal advice.

items.label: Map the processing
items.detail: Identify data, purpose, recipients and systems.

items.label: Confirm the basis
items.detail: Use the institution’s qualified process for applicable requirements.

items.label: Implement safeguards
items.detail: Limit access and support appropriate retention and rights procedures.

items.label: Review changes
items.detail: Check current official notices and operational evidence before real use.

sections.takeaway: Check current official sources with the programme’s authorised privacy owner; the diagram does not certify compliance or update the original legal reading.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. India's DPDP framework — what a non-lawyer must know

sections.title: AI obligations depend on role and use
sections.explanation: A risk-based legal framework cannot be applied from a generic product label alone. Jurisdiction and the actual use matter.

items.label: Use case
items.detail: Describe what the system influences and who is affected.

items.label: Jurisdiction and role
items.detail: Identify the applicable territory and responsibilities.

items.label: Risk and duties
items.detail: Review prohibitions, conditions and documentation with qualified owners.

items.label: Evidence and updates
items.detail: Keep the current official source and the operational review record.

sections.takeaway: Get qualified review of current official requirements; a classroom classification is not a legal determination.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. The EU AI Act and the global direction

sections.title: A team policy turns boundaries into operating rules
sections.explanation: The policy needs clear ownership and procedures people can actually follow, not only a statement that AI should be used responsibly.

items.label: Tools and accounts
items.detail: Name permitted services and who approves a new one.

items.label: Data rules
items.detail: Specify prohibited and conditionally permitted inputs.

items.label: Use and review
items.detail: Define verification, disclosure and approval duties.

items.label: Incidents and ownership
items.detail: Explain reporting, correction, training and periodic review.

sections.takeaway: An approved tool does not mean every dataset or task is approved for it.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Governance you can implement tomorrow: a team AI-use policy

checkpoint.question: Does an organisation-approved AI tool automatically authorise uploading any employee or student record?
checkpoint.answer: No. The purpose, dataset, account arrangement, access and applicable institutional and legal requirements must be approved for the particular use.

m7-pb5.introduction: A second way to understand “Project Block 5 — AI Ethics Audit”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: AI Ethics and Safety Audit: from purpose to evidence
sections.explanation: A scoped, evidence-based review that connects findings to affected people, conditions, owners and a retest date.

items.label: Purpose
items.detail: A scoped, evidence-based review that connects findings to affected people, conditions, owners and a retest date.

items.label: Build an artefact
items.detail: Create the required work for the stated audience and scope.

items.label: Verify and explain
items.detail: Keep test evidence, permissions, limitations and your contribution.

sections.takeaway: Use the full original brief for requirements, timing and marks; this diagram is a companion, not a replacement.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Organise the ai ethics and safety audit evidence pack
sections.explanation: Group the required files so a reviewer can inspect the work and its checks. The detailed checklist above remains unchanged.

items.label: System and stakeholders
items.detail: Define the use, scope, affected people and potential harm.

items.label: Bias and transparency tests
items.detail: Keep the actual paired-run coding sheet and documentation review.

items.label: Privacy and security
items.detail: Map data and permissions and record permitted safety tests.

items.label: Findings and decision
items.detail: Tie each issue to evidence, severity, action and owner.

items.label: Limits and reflection
items.detail: Explain what was not tested and how it constrains the conclusion.

items.label: AI-use statement
items.detail: Separate drafting or tabulation help from your own coding and judgement.

sections.takeaway: Reading the brief is not submission, external project marking or facilitator approval.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Check the boundaries before the build or release
sections.explanation: A good-looking artefact cannot compensate for missing permission, invented evidence or an unsafe action.

items.label: Evidence and scope
items.detail: Use the required real or clearly labelled practice evidence honestly.

items.label: Permission and rights
items.detail: Check relevant data, likeness, music and source permissions.

items.label: Human control
items.detail: Keep the required review before consequential outward effects.

items.label: Test and disclose
items.detail: Record actual results, limitations and AI assistance.

sections.takeaway: Follow the topic-specific constraints in full; a disclosure label does not override the rules.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Plan, build, check and revise
sections.explanation: Use the original suggested schedule to reserve time for review rather than doing all the checking after the final export.

items.label: Plan the scope
items.detail: Start from the actual brief, required outputs and permitted inputs.

items.label: Build deliberately
items.detail: Work in small versions and retain intermediate artefacts.

items.label: Review evidence
items.detail: Run the relevant source, language, functionality and safety checks.

items.label: Revise and submit
items.detail: Record the change and organise the complete evidence package.

sections.takeaway: Keep the process log while working; do not reconstruct fictitious experiments or approvals afterwards.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Make the published criteria inspectable
sections.explanation: The original rubric, weights, pass threshold and any caps remain authoritative. These panels point to the evidence behind its criteria.

items.label: Evidence quality
items.detail: Use actual tests, opened sources and traceable examples.

items.label: Review coverage
items.detail: Consider fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy and security.

items.label: Actionable decision
items.detail: Give scoped conditions, owners and retest dates.

items.label: Clarity and honesty
items.detail: Keep limitations visible and avoid unsupported clearance claims.

sections.takeaway: The animation does not grade work, award marks or override a safety or integrity cap.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Use the review habits, not a success formula
sections.explanation: The original tips are practical prompts for reflection, not guarantees of a result or new assessment conditions.

items.label: Test a narrow use well
items.detail: A focused protocol is more useful than a thin universal verdict.

items.label: Include relevant languages
items.detail: Investigate context-specific differences with the same controlled method.

items.label: Retest a mitigation
items.detail: Keep before/after evidence and the remaining limitation.

sections.takeaway: Choose the habit that addresses your actual weakness and keep evidence of the correction.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Separate tool help from your responsibility
sections.explanation: A useful statement tells the reviewer where assistance entered and what the learner independently checked.

items.label: Name the assistance
items.detail: Identify tools and the tasks for which they were used.

items.label: Trace the evidence
items.detail: State which real sources, tests and outputs were checked.

items.label: Own the judgement
items.detail: Describe selection, revisions, decisions and individual or team contributions.

items.label: Follow the policy
items.detail: Keep assessment restrictions and rights boundaries intact.

sections.takeaway: Disclosure cannot legitimise fabricated evidence, prohibited tool use or missing permission.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can an assistant invent representative test outputs to fill an audit report?
checkpoint.answer: No. Findings must come from actual permitted runs or cited primary evidence. You own the coding, severity judgement and decision.
